units: a charger in use turns warm
current runs through a copper winding inside the device
every conducting material pushes back against the current
that opposition turns part of the energy into heat
a higher power draw raises the share that is wasted
makers provide openings, metal contact parts and sometimes a cooling propeller
a device that runs too hot slows its own pace
a soft object placed under a computer blocks the air openings
text: Touch a charger that has been sitting plugged in all afternoon. It feels warm, and there is nothing mysterious about that. Inside the casing, current travels through slender wires and a copper winding. No conductor carries electricity for free. The material pushes back, and that resistance converts part of the energy into heat. Demand more power from the thing and the wasted portion climbs. Manufacturers understand this perfectly, so they cut ventilation slots into the shell, press metal tabs against the hottest components, and sometimes tuck a miniature fan inside. When the heat cannot escape, the circuits throttle themselves back for their own protection, and the whole machine turns sluggish. That is also why a cushion underneath a laptop suffocates it. The openings are covered, the air stagnates, the temperature climbs. Unplug it, give it room to breathe, and everything settles.

units: dead tablets were piling up in a repair workshop
the devices showed no sign of working at all
the explanation on offer blamed the fault on the battery
the head of the workshop doubted that diagnosis
a teardown revealed a cracked metal joint under the charging connector
a light knock was enough to break that joint
the team built a holder that clamps the board while the joint is rebuilt
the repair became cheap to carry out
the workshop puts its repair notes on public display
text: At a repair counter tucked into the back of a shopping arcade, dead tablets had been stacking up for weeks. The explanation was always the same. Black screen, no response, and a battery blamed for everything. The lead technician never accepted that convenient answer. He opened one unit, then a second, and found a hairline crack in the solder underneath the charging connector, too fine to detect without a magnifier. A knock against a table edge was enough to split it. Rather than swap whole boards, the team built a small jig that clamps the board flat while a hot iron rebuilds the joint. The work now costs almost nothing, and owners walk out with a machine that wakes up again. The shop pins its repair notes to a board beside the door, so people stop discarding a device that a bead of solder can revive.

units: two distinct ways exist for taking apart an old playback device
the first means backing out the screws one at a time
the first calls for marking where each part sat on a sketch
the second means forcing the shell open with a flat tool
the second usually wrecks a clip
the careful way needs a lamp that swivels and a bench swept clear
the bundles of wiring make the gap between the two ways obvious
the text advises taking the careful way
putting it back together runs in the opposite order to taking it apart
text: Before you loosen a single screw, settle on your road, because an old player opens in two different ways. The first belongs to patience. You back out every screw, drop it into a saucer, and mark on a sketch exactly where it lived. The second belongs to nerve. You slide a flat blade beneath the shell, save yourself a minute, and snap a retaining clip. Patience wants a lamp on a bending arm and a workbench swept clear. Nerve wants nothing but a firm wrist. Yet the moment the wiring reveals itself, a pale ribbon glued along the floor of the chassis, the difference opens wide. The patient hand knows where every strand returns. The hasty one tugs at random and tears. Take the first road, then build the machine back together the other way round, and let the tray spring seat itself before the lid comes down.

units: the sorting line described holds three machines that work together
light sensors read the reflection to work out what the packaging is made of
jets of pressurised air push the unwanted pieces aside
that ejection happens without anything touching the objects
belts running at uneven speeds spread the stream and stop pieces from riding on each other
the manager holds that upkeep counts for more than the software
a dirty nozzle bends the path of the ejected pieces
a slack belt upsets the timing of the line
a dusty sensor reads glass as clear plastic
a worker walks the line at intervals to clean it
text: The shed hums on one long note, and the guided tour opens in front of the first sorting line. Three machines operate together there. A row of optical sensors reads the light bouncing off each package and deduces what material it is made of. A rail of compressed air nozzles fires next, knocking unwanted pieces aside within a thousandth of a second, without anything ever touching them. Behind it, belts driven at uneven speeds thin the stream out so that no piece rides on top of another. The plant manager keeps pressing a point that visitors tend to overlook. Reliability rests on maintenance far more than on the software. A clogged nozzle throws the puff off course. A slackened belt drags the timing. A dusty sensor mistakes glass for clear plastic. So an operator walks the line at regular intervals, cloth in hand.

units: the assembly described follows a fixed run of steps
a cut sheet of metal takes its final shape under a press
a coated metal wire laps around a central core
the ends of that winding are stripped of their coating
a magnetic part drops into the ring and is then locked by a collar
the shaft is oiled before it goes in
the turning of the shaft is checked with no load on it
the wires of the winding are held by solder on conducting pads
the shell closes with a seal that keeps dust out
the finished object faces a test under load in a booth
text: Watch an assembly line and a strict order reveals itself, from the opening movement to the last. A cut steel blank arrives on a turntable, and a press stamps the housing shape into it. The winding comes next. Lacquered copper wire feeds off a spool and laps evenly around a core, and its two ends are afterwards stripped bare. A permanent magnet then drops into the outer ring, and a collar locks it into position. The shaft is offered up, oiled, pressed home, and its rotation is checked with no load upon it. Once that reading satisfies, the ends of the winding meet two conducting pads, where a machine deposits a bead of solder. The casing closes last of all, with a supple seal that keeps the dust away. The finished unit travels onward to a testing booth, where a measured load proves that it holds.

units: putting a household appliance back in order has grown hard
shells are now held together with glue rather than screws
the screw heads in use are not sold in ordinary shops
spare parts stop being sold soon after a model reaches the market
the buyer drops the repair and picks up a replacement
objects that half an hour would mend are thrown out
independent workshops close for want of custom
technical skill fades as those workshops shut
some makers show that a cover made to come off adds no bulk
the text calls for standard screws, wiring plans anyone can get and parts kept in stock
text: Mending a household appliance used to be ordinary work. It now takes something close to a feat, and the reasons are not hidden. Makers glue the shells together rather than screw them. They pick screw heads that no ordinary supplier keeps. They stop selling spare parts a short while after a model reaches the shelves. Each choice has a plain result. The owner gives up, buys a replacement, and something half an hour would have mended goes out with the rubbish. Independent workshops close for want of custom, and the skill they carried fades along with them. The old defence about slimness and sealing no longer holds, since some makers show that a cover made to come off adds no bulk at all. Asking for common screws, a wiring plan anyone can get and parts kept in stock is no fond dream. It is what long use costs.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the woman at the centre of the story knew none of the words for machine parts at the start
she taught herself by taking broken toys apart
she runs a small shop wedged between two other businesses
her first trouble came from how awkward her customers felt
the customers were afraid of getting the description of their trouble wrong
she changed the way she takes people in
she opens the device in front of its owner and points at each part while naming it
customers come back having worked out the fault by themselves
the shop is no longer short of custom
text: She says that at the beginning she could not tell a cog from a pulley, and that she taught herself by taking broken toys apart. The neighborhood fixer now runs a narrow shop wedged between a laundry and a florist. Her first difficulty was never the machinery. It was how awkward her customers felt. People would not describe a fault out loud, for fear of saying something foolish. So she changed the way she takes them in. She sets the device on the counter, opens it while its owner watches, and names each component aloud. Here is the catch that sticks. Here is the power socket. Here is the gear that slips. Customers walk out understanding what went wrong. Plenty of them come back later with a fault they have identified themselves, and the shop is never short of customers any more.

units: the two devices compared follow opposite designs
the first puts suction power and toughness first
the first does well on thick woven floor coverings
the first makes a noise that drives the household out
the first leaves dirt in the corners
the second stands out for how well it finds its way about
the second pulls with less force and takes longer to finish the floor
the second steers clear of obstacles and slips under low furniture
the choice hangs on the kind of floor and how crowded the home is
both devices open and empty without a tool
text: Set side by side on a single shelf, two robot vacuums argue for opposite ideas. The first bets on muscle. An eager motor, a broad brush, a roomy bin, and a shell that shrugs off knocks. It shines on deep carpet, but the racket it makes empties the room of its occupants, and its side arm leaves little crescents of grit in the corners. The second bets on judgment. It reads a room accurately, keeps track of its own position, and finds its base without dithering. It pulls less air and needs longer to cover the floor, yet it collides with nothing and slips beneath low furniture. The verdict follows the household. Hard floors and crowded rooms favor the second, thick rugs and open space give the first the advantage. On one count they tie. The bin empties in a second, and the lid lifts without tools.

units: the writer reports on the restoring of a radio set found under the roof
the work splits into three separate jobs
the cabinet was sanded, glued back at one corner and waxed
the inside was covered in a thick deposit
two wires had lost their insulation
the connections were made again wire by wire
the needle on the display no longer follows the turning knob
the writer supposes that a springy part has worn out
the writer promises to write again once the set works
text: You asked how the radio from under the roof was coming along, and I finally owe you a proper account. Three separate pieces of work have kept me occupied. The cabinet came first. I sanded the lifted veneer, glued a corner that had sprung open, and rubbed in a wax that woke the grain of the wood again. The inside came second, and that is where my patience wore thin. Dust lay like grey felt across every valve, and two wires had shed their sleeving entirely. I made the connections again, strand by strand, with fresh wire and a clean joint. The third undertaking holds me still. The needle on the dial refuses to follow the knob, and I suspect a tired spring behind it. When the whole thing is ready, I will stand the set beside the window and write to tell you what the first voice says.

units: a specialist describes the updating of the program held inside a device
the device first checks that the file it received is genuine
the procedure stops if that check fails
the new data is written into an area of memory apart from the one in use
that separation guards the device if the power is cut
the earlier version stays in place until the restart
a counter of attempts sends the start-up back to the old area if the writing fails
the user then notices nothing but a slower start
the prints of the two areas are compared once the switch has happened
the room held by the stale version is won back only after a session with nothing amiss
text: What happens exactly when a machine updates the software held inside it? The engineer we asked walks through the steps in order. First the device checks the signature on the file it received. If the signature fails to match, the process halts on the spot. Next the image is written into a second block of memory, never over the one that is running, so a power cut harms nothing. And the version already there? It stays whole until the machine restarts. What if the writing fails? A retry counter sends the start-up back to the older block, and the user notices nothing but a heavier start. Once the switch has happened, a last check compares the prints of both blocks. The machine frees the room held by the stale version only after one full session with nothing amiss. That caution explains why the job seems to drag.
